p.src: Now, as Lin Chong was strolling idly along that day, someone suddenly called to him from behind. He turned and recognized the tavern waiter Li Xiao’er. When they had both been in the Eastern Capital, Lin Chong had often looked after him. Back then in the Eastern Capital, Li Xiao’er had foolishly stolen property belonging to his employer. He was caught and was about to be handed over to the authorities for punishment. But Lin Chong intervened and pleaded for him, thereby saving him from being handed over to the authorities. He also paid some money on his behalf, and only then was Li Xiao’er released from the affair. Unable to remain in the capital, Li Xiao’er had again depended on Lin Chong to provide traveling expenses so that he might seek refuge with someone elsewhere. Neither had expected to meet the other here today. Lin Chong said, “Brother Xiao’er, how did you come to be here?” Li Xiao’er bowed and said, “Ever since my benefactor rescued me and furnished me with traveling expenses, I have wandered from place to place without finding anyone who would take me in. In the course of my travels I unexpectedly reached Cangzhou and sought employment at an inn whose proprietor was named Wang. He kept me on as a waiter. Seeing that I worked diligently, prepared good dishes, and blended fine sauces, while all the customers praised my fare, the business prospered. My employer had a daughter, so he took me into the family as his son-in-law. Now both my father-in-law and mother-in-law are dead. Only my wife and I remain, and for the present we run a tea-and-wine shop before the prison camp. I had come this way to collect a debt when I met you, my benefactor. But what has brought you here, my benefactor?” Pointing to the brand on his face, Lin Chong said, “Because I offended Grand Marshal Gao, he contrived trouble and framed me. I was prosecuted, branded, and banished here. They have now placed me in charge of the Hall of the Heavenly King, though I do not know what will become of me in the end. I never expected to meet you here today.” Li Xiao’er invited Lin Chong home and seated him inside, then called his wife out to pay homage to their benefactor. The couple said joyfully, “We have no family or kin to rely upon. For our benefactor to come today is as though you had descended from heaven.” Lin Chong said, “I am a convicted prisoner. I fear my presence may bring disgrace upon you both.” Li Xiao’er replied, “Who has not heard the great name of our benefactor? You must not speak so. Whenever you have clothes that need tending, bring them here, and we shall wash, starch, and mend them for you.” They entertained Lin Chong with food and wine, and at night escorted him back to the Hall of the Heavenly King. The next day they invited him again. From then on Lin Chong frequented the waiter’s home, while the couple often brought soup and drink to the camp for him. Seeing how respectfully and devotedly the couple treated him, Lin Chong would often give them some silver to add to their business capital.

p.src: But let us leave these incidental matters and return to the main story. Time sped swiftly by, and winter soon arrived. Lin Chong’s padded clothes, trousers, and jackets were all put in order and mended by Li Xiao’er’s wife. One day, while Li Xiao’er was at the entrance preparing vegetables and dishes, a man suddenly slipped inside and sat down in the tavern. A second man slipped in directly behind him. On closer inspection, the first was dressed as a military officer, while the second looked like a servant and followed him to take a seat. Li Xiao’er went in and asked, “Would you gentlemen care for wine?” The first man took out a tael of silver and gave it to Xiao’er, saying, “Put this aside at the counter for now and bring us three or four flasks of good wine. When our guests arrive, keep bringing fruit, wine, and food without waiting to be asked.” Li Xiao’er asked, “Whom are you inviting, sir?” The man replied, “Trouble yourself to go to the prison camp and invite the governor and the warder here for a talk. If they ask, say only that a gentleman wishes to speak with them and discuss some business, and is waiting especially for them.”

p.src: Li Xiao’er agreed and went to the prison camp, where he first invited the warder; then together they went to the governor’s residence and invited him, and all returned to the tavern. The officer exchanged formal greetings with the governor and the warder. The governor said, “We have never met before. May I ask your honored surname and name?” The man replied, “I have a letter here; you will know shortly. For now, bring the wine.” Li Xiao’er hurriedly opened the wine and laid out vegetables, fruit, and other dishes. The man called for a ceremonial tray, poured the cups, invited the others to drink, and had them take their seats. Xiao’er, alone, darted back and forth like a shuttle, too busy serving them to pause. The servant who had followed the officer asked for a vessel of hot water and warmed the wine himself. After they had drunk a dozen or more cups, he ordered further dishes to accompany the wine and set them on the table. Then the officer said, “I have my own attendant to warm the wine. Do not come unless I call you. We have matters to discuss in private.”

p.src: Li Xiao’er assented and returned to the entrance, where he called his wife and said, “My dear, there is something suspicious about those two men.” His wife asked, “What is suspicious about them?” Xiao’er said, “From their speech and accents, those two men are from the Eastern Capital. At first they did not know the governor, yet later, when I carried in the dishes, I heard the warder let slip the three words ‘Grand Marshal Gao.’ Could these men have some design concerning Arms Instructor Lin? I shall keep watch here at the entrance. You go behind the private room and listen to what they are saying.” His wife said, “Why not go to the camp, fetch Arms Instructor Lin, and have him identify them?” Li Xiao’er replied, “You do not understand. Arms Instructor Lin is quick-tempered; at the slightest provocation he will kill men and set fires. Suppose I bring him here and he finds that one of them really is that Marshal Lu he spoke of the other day—would he ever let the matter rest? If he causes trouble, you and I will surely be implicated. Just go and listen first; then we shall decide what to do.” His wife said, “You are right.” She went inside and listened for about two hours. Coming out, she said, “The three or four of them kept whispering with their heads together, and I could not make out what they were saying. But I saw the man dressed as an officer take a bundle wrapped in a handkerchief from his attendant’s breast and hand it to the governor and the warder. What was inside must surely have been gold or silver. Then I heard the warder say, ‘Leave everything to me. One way or another, I shall finish him off.’”

p.src: At once Lin Chong asked, “What urgent matter is it?” Li Xiao’er invited Lin Chong inside to sit down and said, “Just now a suspicious fellow from the Eastern Capital came here and treated the commandant and the warder to wine for half the day. The warder let the three words ‘Grand Marshal Gao’ slip from his lips, which made me suspicious. I had my wife listen for an hour, but they whispered in one another’s ears, and she could not hear what they were saying. At the end, she heard only the warder answer, ‘Leave it all to the two of us. One way or another, we’ll finish him off.’ Those two then handed a parcel of gold and silver to the commandant and the warder. After another round of wine, they all went their separate ways. I do not know who the men were, but I have my suspicions and fear they may mean harm to you, my benefactor.” Lin Chong said, “What did the man look like?” Li Xiao’er replied, “He was short in stature, with a fair, clean-shaven face, and looked to be a little over thirty. His attendant was not tall either and had a dark ruddy complexion.” Lin Chong was greatly startled when he heard this. “The man in his thirties must be Warden Lu. That vile scoundrel has dared come here to murder me! He had better not cross my path, or I’ll pound his flesh and bones to pulp!” Li Xiao’er said, “You need only guard against him. Have you not heard the old saying, ‘Beware of choking when you eat, and of stumbling when you walk’?”

p.src: Furious, Lin Chong left Li Xiao’er’s house. First he went to the market and bought a sharp wrist-cutting dagger, which he carried on his person. He searched everywhere, through the main streets and back alleys. Li Xiao’er and his wife broke into a cold sweat for fear of what might happen. Nothing happened that night. At daybreak the next morning, after rising and washing, he took his dagger and again searched all day through Cangzhou, inside and outside the walls, circling through every narrow street and alley. There was no stir at all in the prison camp. Lin Chong returned to Li Xiao’er and said, “Again, nothing happened today.” Xiao’er replied, “Benefactor, I can only hope it remains so. Just be careful yourself.” Lin Chong returned alone to the Temple of the Heavenly King and passed the night there. For another three or five days he searched the streets, but when he saw no sign of anything, he gradually let down his guard.

p.src: On the sixth day, the commandant summoned Lin Chong to the inspection hall and said, “You have been here a good while, yet out of regard for Master Chai I have never done anything to advance you. Fifteen li beyond the eastern gate stands the army fodder depot. Whenever grass and feed are delivered each month, there are customary fees to be collected. An old soldier was originally assigned to watch it. I shall now favor you by sending you to replace him, while he comes back to guard the Temple of the Heavenly King. You can earn a few strings of cash there for your expenses. Go there with the warder and make the handover.” Lin Chong answered, “I shall go at once.” He left the camp and went straight to Li Xiao’er’s house, where he told the couple, “Today the commandant assigned me to take charge of the army fodder depot. What do you make of it?” Li Xiao’er said, “That post is much like the one at the Temple of the Heavenly King. When grass and feed are received there, you can collect some customary fees. Ordinarily, no one can obtain that post without spending money for it.” Lin Chong said, “Instead of harming me, they have given me a good post. I truly cannot fathom their purpose.” Li Xiao’er replied, “Benefactor, do not be suspicious. So long as nothing happens, all the better. Only my home will be far from you. After some time, I shall find a chance to come and visit.” He prepared several cups of wine at home and invited Lin Chong to drink.

p.src: Lin Chong and the warder found nowhere along the road to buy wine, and before long they reached the outside of the fodder depot. Looking it over, they saw a low yellow-earth wall encircling the place and a pair of large gates. When they pushed the gates open and looked inside, they saw seven or eight thatched huts serving as granaries, stacks of horse fodder on every side, and two thatched halls in the middle. When they entered one of the halls, they found the old soldier inside warming himself by the fire. The warder said, “The commandant has sent this man, Lin Chong, to replace you. You are to return and guard the Temple of the Heavenly King. Make the handover at once.” The old soldier took the keys and led Lin Chong around, explaining, “The granaries bear the official seals. Every one of these stacks of fodder has been counted.” The old soldier showed him the tally of all the stacks and then led him into the thatched hall. After gathering his belongings, he said before departing, “I shall leave the brazier, pot, bowls, and plates for you to use.” Lin Chong said, “I have some of my own at the Temple of the Heavenly King. If you need these, take them with you.” The old soldier pointed to a large gourd hanging on the wall and said, “If you want to buy wine, leave the depot and follow the eastern highway for two or three li. You will find a market settlement there.” The old soldier then returned to the camp with the warder.

p.src: Now Lin Chong set his bundle and bedding on the bed, sat down, and kindled a small fire. Beside the hut lay a pile of firewood and charcoal; he took a few pieces and lit them in the hearth. Looking up at the thatched hut, he saw that it was crumbling on every side; moreover, the north wind battered it until the whole structure shook. Lin Chong said, “How can this hut last through the winter? When the snow clears, I shall go into town and summon a mason to repair it.” After warming himself for a while, he still felt chilled and thought, “That old soldier just said there was a market two li away. Why not go and buy some wine?” He took some small pieces of silver from his bundle, slung the wine gourd from his flowered spear, covered the glowing coals, put on his felt hat, took the key, went out, and pulled the door of the thatched hall shut behind him; at the main entrance, he pulled the two gates of the fodder yard closed and locked them; then, carrying the key, he set off eastward at an easy pace. He trod through shattered jade and scattered jewels in the snow, making his way onward with the north wind at his back. The snow was falling heavily. Before he had gone much more than half a li, he saw an old temple. Lin Chong bowed and said, “May the deity protect me. Another day I shall return to burn paper offerings.” After walking a while longer, he saw a cluster of houses. Lin Chong stopped to look and noticed a little straw broom hanging out in the open inside a fence. Lin Chong went straight into the tavern. The proprietor asked, “Where have you come from, traveler?” Lin Chong said, “Do you recognize this gourd?” The proprietor looked at it and said, “This gourd belongs to the old soldier at the fodder yard.” Lin Chong said, “So it does.” The proprietor said, “Since you are the good fellow now guarding the fodder yard, please sit a while. The weather is cold, so have three cups as a modest welcome.” The tavern keeper sliced a plate of cooked beef, warmed a pot of wine, and invited Lin Chong to partake. Lin Chong bought some more beef himself and drank several more cups. Then he bought another gourdful of wine, wrapped up the two pieces of beef, and left some small silver behind. He slung the wine gourd from his flowered spear, tucked the beef inside his robe, thanked them for their hospitality, passed through the gate in the fence, and set off home again, this time facing the north wind. By evening, the snow was falling harder than ever. In ancient times a scholar composed a lyric expressly lamenting the misery that snow brings upon the poor:

After walking a while longer, he saw a cluster of houses. Lin Chong stopped to look and noticed a little straw broom hanging out in the open inside a fence.
Lin Chong went straight into the tavern. The proprietor asked, “Where have you come from, traveler?”
Lin Chong said, “Do you recognize this gourd?”
The proprietor looked at it and said, “This gourd belongs to the old soldier at the fodder yard.”
Lin Chong said, “So it does.”
The proprietor said, “Since you are the good fellow now guarding the fodder yard, please sit a while.
The weather is cold, so have three cups as a modest welcome.”
The tavern keeper sliced a plate of cooked beef, warmed a pot of wine, and invited Lin Chong to partake.
Lin Chong bought some more beef himself and drank several more cups.
Then he bought another gourdful of wine, wrapped up the two pieces of beef, and left some small silver behind.

He slung the wine gourd from his flowered spear, tucked the beef inside his robe, thanked them for their hospitality, passed through the gate in the fence, and set off home again, this time facing the north wind.
By evening, the snow was falling harder than ever.
In ancient times a scholar composed a lyric expressly lamenting the misery that snow brings upon the poor:

p.src: The bitter wind from the vast north scours the earth; how splendidly this snow comes down! Fluff teased and wadding torn, flakes cut as broad as great baskets. Among the woods, bamboo huts and thatched cottages are all but crushed beneath it. Yet wealthy and mighty households complain there is still too little to suppress the pestilential vapors. They warm themselves at red braziers burning fragrant beast-shaped charcoal and dress in padded robes and quilted coats. Plucking plum blossoms in their hands, they sing that it is an auspicious sign for the realm, never sparing a thought for the humble poor. Recluses lie at ease in lofty chambers, composing many drafts of verse.

p.src: To resume: Lin Chong trod through the auspicious snow and faced the north wind, hurrying as though in flight to the gate of the fodder yard. He unlocked it and went inside, only to cry out in dismay. Truly, Heaven’s justice was manifest, protecting a good and righteous man. For this great snowfall had saved Lin Chong’s life. The two-roomed thatched hall had already collapsed beneath the snow. Lin Chong thought, “What am I to do?” He laid his flowered spear and gourd down in the snow. Fearing that live coals in the brazier might start a spreading fire, he moved aside a section of broken wall and thrust half his body inside to feel about. The embers in the brazier had all been extinguished by the melted snow. When Lin Chong felt about on the bed, he managed to pull out only a single padded quilt. He crawled back out and saw that darkness had fallen. He thought, “There is nowhere even to make a fire. How shall I manage?” Then he remembered, “Half a li from here stands an old temple where I can shelter. I shall spend the night there and decide what to do at daybreak.” He rolled up the quilt, slung the wine gourd from his flowered spear, pulled the gate shut as before, locked it, and headed toward the temple. Once through the temple gate, he closed it behind him. There was only a large stone nearby, so he lifted it over and propped it against the gate. Inside, he saw upon the hall a gilded statue of the Mountain God in armor, flanked by a judge on one side and a little demon on the other; a pile of paper offerings lay to one side. Looking all around, he found neither neighboring houses nor a temple keeper. Lin Chong set his spear and wine gourd upon the pile of paper and spread out the padded quilt. First he removed his felt hat, shook all the snow from his body, and took off the white outer shirt he wore over his clothes. It was already half soaked, so he placed it together with the felt hat upon the altar table; then he pulled the quilt over the lower half of his body. He lifted the gourd of cold wine and drank slowly, eating the beef from inside his robe as a relish.

p.src: Snow challenged the force of the flames, while grass magnified their fury. The wind over the grass was cause enough for dread; stranger still, there was fuel delivered amid the snow. Red dragons leapt and battled—how could the flakes of jade armor prevail? White butterflies vied in flight, yet could scarcely conceal the blazing fire-lotuses. At first one might think the Lord of Fire had loosed his divine steeds to graze in this place; or suppose that the Vermilion Bird, driven from the south, was building nests everywhere. Who knew disaster would arise upon innocent ground? Yet one must believe that even in a darkened chamber, Heaven opens its lightning eye. The sight of this fire could kindle a brave man’s wrath; confronted with this snow, the treacherous and wicked should tremble in their hearts.

p.src: At once Lin Chong seized his flowered spear and was about to open the door and fight the fire when he heard voices outside. Lin Chong crouched by the door and listened. The footsteps of three men sounded, coming straight toward the temple. They pushed at the door, but the stone braced it, and they could not force it open. The three men stood beneath the temple eaves and watched the fire. One of them said, “What do you think of this scheme?” Another replied, “It is all thanks to the commandant and the prison warden for taking such pains! When I return to the capital and report to the Grand Marshal, I guarantee that both of you will be made high officials. This time Instructor Zhang will have no excuse to offer.” The first man said, “Now that we have finally disposed of Lin Chong, young Master Gao is certain to recover from his illness.” Another said, “That scoundrel Instructor Zhang has had people approach him time and again, saying, ‘Your son-in-law is gone.’ But Instructor Zhang grew ever more unwilling to consent. Because of that, the young master’s illness has steadily worsened. So the Grand Marshal expressly sent the two of us to beg you gentlemen to carry this out. And now, unexpectedly, it has all been accomplished.” Another said, “I personally climbed over the wall and lit more than ten fires among the haystacks on every side. Where could he possibly escape?” The other said, “By now, eight-tenths of him must have burned away.” Then another was heard to say, “Even if he escapes with his life, he will still be sentenced to death for letting the army’s fodder yard burn.” Another said, “Let us go back to the city.” One replied, “Let us watch a little longer. If we can pick up a bone or two of his and take them back to the capital, then when we meet the Grand Marshal and the young master at the residence, we can show that we know how to get a job done.”

p.src: From their voices, Lin Chong recognized the three men as the prison officer, Adjutant Lu, and Fu An. He thought, “Heaven has taken pity on Lin Chong! Had the thatched hall not collapsed, those villains would surely have burned me alive.” Quietly moving the stone aside, he leveled his tasseled spear, pulled open the temple door with his left hand, and roared, “Where do you think you’re going, you scoundrels?” The three tried desperately to flee, but were so stunned that they froze where they stood. Lin Chong raised his arm and, with one cracking thrust, struck down the prison officer first. Adjutant Lu cried, “Spare my life!” His limbs failed him from terror, and he could not run. Fu An had not gone ten paces before Lin Chong caught him and drove the spear into his back, felling him too. Lin Chong wheeled around. Adjutant Lu had managed only three or four steps when Lin Chong shouted, “You villain! Where do you think you’re going?” Seizing him by the chest, Lin Chong flung him onto the snow. He planted his spear in the ground, pinned Lu’s chest beneath his foot, drew the knife at his side, and laid it against Lu Qian’s face. “You wretch! I have never borne you any grudge. Why have you persecuted me so? Murder itself might be pardoned, but what you have done defies all human justice.” Adjutant Lu pleaded, “It was none of my doing. The Grand Marshal ordered me here, and I dared not disobey.” Lin Chong cursed him. “Treacherous dog! We have known each other since childhood, yet today you came to murder me. How can you say it was none of your doing? Taste my blade!” He tore open Lu Qian’s upper garments and plunged the pointed knife into his heart. Blood burst from all seven orifices as Lin Chong tore out his heart and liver and held them in his hand. Looking back, he saw the prison officer scrambling to his feet to escape. Lin Chong pinned him down and shouted, “So you too were this wicked! Taste my blade as well.” In an instant he cut off the man’s head and impaled it on his spear. Then he returned and cut off the heads of Fu An and Lu Qian as well. Sheathing his pointed knife, he tied the three men’s hair together, carried their heads into the temple, and arranged them on the offering table before the Mountain God. He put on his white cloth shirt again, fastened his sash, donned his felt hat, and drained all the cold wine in his gourd. He discarded both the quilt and the gourd, took up his spear, left the temple, and headed east. Before he had gone three or five li, he saw villagers nearby hurrying to fight the fire with buckets and hooks. Lin Chong told them, “Hurry and put out the fire. I am going to report it to the authorities.” He pressed onward with his spear in hand. A poem bears witness:

p.src: Heaven’s justice shines too brightly to deny; never make wicked treachery your worthy plan. Had wind and snow not sent him out for village wine, he surely would have burned to lifeless ash. p.src: The snow fell ever more fiercely. Lin Chong walked eastward for two watches, but his clothes were thin, and he could no longer endure the cold. Looking about across the snow, he saw that he was now far from the fodder depot. Deep within a sparse wood ahead, amid tangled trees, he saw several thatched cottages in the distance, weighed down by snow, with firelight shining through cracks in their broken walls. Lin Chong went straight toward the cottages. He pushed open the door and saw an elderly tenant seated in the middle, with four or five younger farmhands sitting around him warming themselves. Firewood blazed brightly in the sunken hearth. Lin Chong stepped forward and said, “Greetings, gentlemen. I am an attendant from the prison camp. The snow has soaked my clothes, so I beg your leave to dry them by this fire.” A tenant replied, “Go ahead and warm yourself. What harm could it do?” As Lin Chong warmed his wet clothes, they grew somewhat dry. Then he noticed a little jar nestled beside the coals, from which came the fragrance of wine. Lin Chong said, “I have a little silver with me. Would you trouble yourselves to sell me some wine?” The old tenant said, “Each night we take turns guarding the grain bins. It is the fourth watch now and bitterly cold. There is scarcely enough for us few, so how could we sell any to you? Do not expect any!” Lin Chong said again, “At least sell me two or three bowls—anything will do—to ward off the cold.” The old tenant said, “Stop pestering us, you fellow.” The fragrance only sharpened Lin Chong’s thirst. “I cannot help myself,” he said. “Spare me a little.” The tenants said, “We kindly let you warm yourself and dry your clothes, and now you demand our wine! Be off with you! If you will not go, we shall hang you up here.” Lin Chong said angrily, “What unreasonable wretches you are!” With his spear he flicked up a blazing piece of firewood toward the old tenant’s face, then thrust the spear into the hearth and stirred it violently. The old man’s beard caught fire and blazed, and all the tenants leaped to their feet. Lin Chong lashed about with the shaft of his spear, and the old tenant fled first; the others were powerless to resist. Lin Chong chased and thrashed them until they all ran away.

p.src: Lin Chong said, “Now they are all gone, this lord can enjoy his wine in peace.” There were two coconut-shell dippers on the earthen platform. He took one down, poured wine from the jar, and drank for a while, leaving half behind. Taking up his spear, he went out and continued on his way. He lurched along, one step high and the next low, staggering without command of his feet. Before he had gone a single li, a blast of north wind knocked him down beside a mountain stream, and there was no getting up again. As a rule, once a drunken man falls, he cannot rise. And so Lin Chong lay drunk in the snow.

p.src: Meanwhile, the tenants returned with more than twenty men, dragging spears and carrying staves. When they rushed to the thatched cottage, Lin Chong was nowhere to be seen. Following his tracks, they pursued him and found him lying in the snow, his tasseled spear cast aside. The tenants rushed upon him together, hauled him up where he lay, and bound him with a rope. During the fifth watch, they escorted the bound Lin Chong to a certain place. It was no ordinary place, and events there would cause thousands of warships and armored vessels to be arrayed fore and aft within Smartweed Marsh; and scores upon hundreds of valiant heroes to stand on either side within the stronghold of the Marshes. Truly, the killing aura chills a man whenever the tale is told, and its mournful wind pierces to the bone wherever it is recounted. But to learn where the tenants took Lin Chong, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
